html:
The Manteño-Huancavilca culture was one of the last pre-Columbian cultures of coastal Ecuador, active from about 850 to 1600. It covered the coast of Manabí and the Gulf of Guayaquil, the same area as the much older Valdivia culture.

The Manteño were seafaring traders. They sailed large balsa wood rafts with cotton sails along the Pacific coast, carrying Spondylus shells, which Andean peoples prized for rituals, as far as Peru and probably western Mexico. They made U-shaped stone seats, likely for chiefs, and lived in large towns on the coast.

In 1526 the pilot of Francisco Pizarro captured one of their trading rafts at sea, loaded with gold, silver, cloth and shells. It was the first clear sign to the Spanish of the riches of the Inca world to the south. Spanish conquest and disease ended the culture by about 1600.
